newsitem.title: UK: Upbeat Glaxo wins strong analyst approval.
newsitem.headline: Upbeat Glaxo wins strong analyst approval.

text.p: Bold forecasts by British drugs giant Glaxo Wellcome Plc that it would return to double digit sales growth by the end of the century were given strong backing by analysts on Thursday.

The company, which is confident that it will ride out the loss of U.S. and British patents on blockbuster ulcer treatment Zantac later this year, has promised double digit sales growth in 1999 after "low single digit" growth in 1997 and 1998 as generic competition erodes Zantac's position.
Analysts said managers put in an impressive performance at a meeting following 1996 results, doing much to restore confidence.

Paul Diggle, director of equity research at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull, said Glaxo Wellcome had gone a long way to answer the question of whether it was "a becalmed giant that through patent expiries is going to be hard-pressed to grow... or a serious growth player which faces a bit of a dip."

Analysts said the company's decision to stress the worst-case scenario for Zantac, which included saying that sales in the key U.S. market could plunge by up to 80 percent in the 12 months from July 1997, underlined Glaxo Wellcome's confidence in the growth of other products.

Barclays de Zoete Wedd (BZW) analyst Steve Plag said the management had "demolished the view that gained ground at the end of last year that the company wouldn't be capable of double digit sales growth."

Plag said the forecast was "very credible," pointing to the 14 percent sales growth excluding Zantac last year and to the Glaxo's plans to introduce 20 new products between now and 2000. "Twenty (products) over four years is phenomenal," Plag said.

Williams de Broe analyst Peter Cartwright was impressed by the 50 percent growth in sales of products launched since 1990. "It is quite a quality message on those new products," he said, adding: "They have certainly clarified their stance and put down a marker on sales and earnings."

SocGen's Diggle said Glaxo Wellcome's migraine drug Imigran and its portfolios of AIDs and asthma products would lead the renaissance, and added: "they are all growing in market segments that have very strong underlying growth rates."
A note of caution on the sales forecast was added by Stephen Putnam of Kleinwort Benson.
"It is quite early to be saying that for 1999," he said, adding: "I don't think many companies would want to be caught making that sort of prediction."
Putnam said he was preparing to shave his earnings forecasts for the group through to the end of the century, principally because of concerns over profit margins.

"They appear to be saying that the cost structure will be rather different. In two years time it will look more like a conventional drugs company with a very wide spread of products, and not many of those have 37 percent margins," Putnam said.

He is reducing his 1997 earnings per share (eps) forecast to 54.0 pence from 56.0 pence, giving a pre-tax profit figure of 2.8 billion stg instead of 2.9 billion. Looking ahead to 1999 he said he was likely to cut the eps estimate to 62.0 pence from 63.5 pence.

SocGen's Diggle said he would cut his forecast for 1997 pre-tax profit to 2.825 billion stg from 2.900 largely as a result of currency impacts, while Williams de Broe's Cartwright said his 1997 forecast of 3.030 billion stg would "not change substantially."
Cartwright, Diggle and Plag said they were all buyers of the stock, noting that Glaxo Wellcome traded at a discount to most of its U.S. and European competitors.

"It has always been a good time to buy a drugs company just before a patent expiry," said Plag, who added that after this year Glaxo Wellcome faced no major patent expiry until well into the next decade, unlike most of its rivals.
"We think that by the end of 1998 Glaxo Wellcome will be one of the strongest drug companies in the industry," he added.
